claim: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH), pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons are satiety signaling (anorexigenic).
source: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH) satiety signaling (anorexigenic) pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing and hunger signaling (orexigenic) agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons are key components of the neuronal circuits that control food intake and energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about POMC neurons in the ARH.

claim: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH), agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons are hunger signaling (orexigenic).
source: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH) satiety signaling (anorexigenic) pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing and hunger signaling (orexigenic) agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons are key components of the neuronal circuits that control food intake and energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AgRP neurons in the ARH.

claim: POMC-expressing and AgRP-expressing neurons are key components of the neuronal circuits that control food intake and energy homeostasis.
source: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH) satiety signaling (anorexigenic) pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing and hunger signaling (orexigenic) agouti-related peptide (AgRP)-expressing neurons are key components of the neuronal circuits that control food intake and energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction and supported by references.

claim: Noradrenalin increases the activity of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Perforated patch clamp recordings showed that noradrenalin changes the activity of these functionally antagonistic neurons in opposite ways, increasing the activity of the orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons and decreasing the activity of the anorexigenic POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by perforated patch clamp recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Noradrenalin decreases the activity of anorexigenic POMC neurons.
source: Perforated patch clamp recordings showed that noradrenalin changes the activity of these functionally antagonistic neurons in opposite ways, increasing the activity of the orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons and decreasing the activity of the anorexigenic POMC neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by perforated patch clamp recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The opposing effect of noradrenalin on NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons is mediated by the activation of excitatory α1A- and β-adrenergic receptors in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Cell type-specific transcriptomics and pharmacological experiments revealed that the opposing effect on these neurons is mediated by the activation of excitatory α1A - and β- adrenergic receptors in NPY/AgRP neurons, while POMC neurons are inhibited via α2A – adrenergic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type-specific transcriptomics and pharmacological experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: POMC neurons are inhibited via α2A-adrenergic receptors.
source: Cell type-specific transcriptomics and pharmacological experiments revealed that the opposing effect on these neurons is mediated by the activation of excitatory α1A - and β- adrenergic receptors in NPY/AgRP neurons, while POMC neurons are inhibited via α2A – adrenergic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type-specific transcriptomics and pharmacological experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The coordinated differential modulation of the key hypothalamic neurons in control of energy homeostasis assigns noradrenalin an important role to promote feeding.
source: Thus, the coordinated differential modulation of the key hypothalamic neurons in control of energy homeostasis assigns noradrenalin an important role to promote feeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing opposite effects on orexigenic and anorexigenic neurons.

claim: Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms mediating information processing in neuronal circuits that regulate energy homeostasis is essential to devise specific pharmacological strategies for obese patients.
source: Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms mediating information processing in neuronal circuits that regulate energy homeostasis is essential to devise specific pharmacological strategies, which assist obese patients in starting and maintaining a program of weight loss with no or minimized side effects on other neuronal systems (Gouni-Berthold et al., 2013; Holes-Lewis et al., 2013; Misra, 2013).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Important microcircuits in control of energy balance are localized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH).
source: Important microcircuits in control of energy balance are localized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH), which contains two main neuron populations with antagonistic functions: Neuropeptide Y and agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) co-expressing neurons signaling hunger, promoting food intake, and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) - expressing neurons which signal satiety (Sohn et al., 2013; Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NPY/AgRP co-expressing neurons signal hunger and promote food intake.
source: Important microcircuits in control of energy balance are localized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH), which contains two main neuron populations with antagonistic functions: Neuropeptide Y and agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) co-expressing neurons signaling hunger, promoting food intake, and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) - expressing neurons which signal satiety (Sohn et al., 2013; Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: POMC-expressing neurons signal satiety.
source: Important microcircuits in control of energy balance are localized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARH), which contains two main neuron populations with antagonistic functions: Neuropeptide Y and agouti-related peptide (NPY/AgRP) co-expressing neurons signaling hunger, promoting food intake, and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) - expressing neurons which signal satiety (Sohn et al., 2013; Varela and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Insulin is an important fuel-sensing endocrine and metabolic factor that modulates POMC and AgRP neurons.
source: Many important fuel-sensing endocrine and metabolic factors, such as insulin, leptin, glucose, serotonin, dopamine, free fatty acids and uridine diphosphate (Gao and Horvath, 2007; Jo et al., 2009; Jordan et al., 2010; Sohn et al., 2011; Steculorum et al., 2015; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang and van den Pol, 2016) have been identified and various immediate actions of these modulators and nutrient components on the POMC and AgRP neurons are well understood (Belgardt et al., 2008; Claret et al., 2007; Jo et al., 2009; Parton et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 1997, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Leptin is an important fuel-sensing endocrine and metabolic factor that modulates POMC and AgRP neurons.
source: Many important fuel-sensing endocrine and metabolic factors, such as insulin, leptin, glucose, serotonin, dopamine, free fatty acids and uridine diphosphate (Gao and Horvath, 2007; Jo et al., 2009; Jordan et al., 2010; Sohn et al., 2011; Steculorum et al., 2015; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang and van den Pol, 2016) have been identified and various immediate actions of these modulators and nutrient components on the POMC and AgRP neurons are well understood (Belgardt et al., 2008; Claret et al., 2007; Jo et al., 2009; Parton et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 1997, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Glucose is an important fuel-sensing endocrine and metabolic factor that modulates POMC and AgRP neurons.
source: Many important fuel-sensing endocrine and metabolic factors, such as insulin, leptin, glucose, serotonin, dopamine, free fatty acids and uridine diphosphate (Gao and Horvath, 2007; Jo et al., 2009; Jordan et al., 2010; Sohn et al., 2011; Steculorum et al., 2015; Varela and Horvath, 2012; Zhang and van den Pol, 2016) have been identified and various immediate actions of these modulators and nutrient components on the POMC and AgRP neurons are well understood (Belgardt et al., 2008; Claret et al., 2007; Jo et al., 2009; Parton et al., 2007; Spanswick et al., 1997, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effect of the catecholamine noradrenalin on the ARH is not well defined.
source: However, the effect of the catecholamine noradrenalin (NA) on the ARH is not well defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Noradrenalin is associated with energy homeostasis and food intake.
source: Noradrenalin is associated with a number of important CNS functions (Szabadi, 2013) including energy homeostasis and food intake (Commins et al., 1999; Ste Marie et al., 2005; Thomas and Palmiter, 1997; Wellman, 2005, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Noradrenergic projections from the hindbrain (A1, A2 noradrenergic cell groups) to the ARH have been described in rats.
source: Potentially, NA could be a direct modulator of the energy homeostasis-regulatory POMC- and AgRP neurons in the ARH, since noradrenergic projections from the hindbrain (A1, A2 noradrenergic cell groups) and the locus coeruleus (LC) to the ARH have been described in rats (Fraley, 2006; Fraley and Ritter, 2003; Yoon et al., 2013) and manipulation of the noradrenergic system in the hypothalamus has been found to modify feeding behavior and food intake.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in rats.

claim: Noradrenergic projections from the locus coeruleus (LC) to the ARH have been described in rats.
source: Potentially, NA could be a direct modulator of the energy homeostasis-regulatory POMC- and AgRP neurons in the ARH, since noradrenergic projections from the hindbrain (A1, A2 noradrenergic cell groups) and the locus coeruleus (LC) to the ARH have been described in rats (Fraley, 2006; Fraley and Ritter, 2003; Yoon et al., 2013) and manipulation of the noradrenergic system in the hypothalamus has been found to modify feeding behavior and food intake.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in rats.

claim: Manipulation of the noradrenergic system in the hypothalamus has been found to modify feeding behavior and food intake.
source: Potentially, NA could be a direct modulator of the energy homeostasis-regulatory POMC- and AgRP neurons in the ARH, since noradrenergic projections from the hindbrain (A1, A2 noradrenergic cell groups) and the locus coeruleus (LC) to the ARH have been described in rats (Fraley, 2006; Fraley and Ritter, 2003; Yoon et al., 2013) and manipulation of the noradrenergic system in the hypothalamus has been found to modify feeding behavior and food intake.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Impairment of the dorsal noradrenergic bundle caused hyperphagia.
source: Impairment of the dorsal or the ventral noradrenergic bundle, which contain efferent projections from the LC to the forebrain, caused hyper- or hypophagia, respectively (Ahlskog and Hoebel, 1973; Hoebel et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion experiments.

claim: Impairment of the ventral noradrenergic bundle caused hypophagia.
source: Impairment of the dorsal or the ventral noradrenergic bundle, which contain efferent projections from the LC to the forebrain, caused hyper- or hypophagia, respectively (Ahlskog and Hoebel, 1973; Hoebel et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion experiments.

claim: Local NA injections into defined hypothalamus regions either elicits or inhibits feeding in rodents.
source: In line with these lesion experiments, local NA injections into defined hypothalamus regions either elicits or inhibits feeding in rodents (Booth, 1967; Leibowitz, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The NA effect on feeding behavior is versatile and site-specific.
source: These findings not only demonstrate noradrenergic modulation of food intake, but also indicate that the NA effect on feeding behavior is versatile and site-specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited lesion and injection experiments showing different effects in different locations.

claim: Unidentified ARH neurons in rats responded to NA application in extracellular recordings.
source: Additional evidence that NA is associated with the regulation of the homeostatic system in the ARH came from extracellular recordings of unidentified ARH neurons in rats, which responded to NA application (Kang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NA increases the expression of Agrp and Npy mRNA in the rat ARH in response to glucoprivation.
source: Furthermore, NA increases the expression of Agrp and Npy mRNA in the rat ARH in response to glucoprivation (Fraley and Ritter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The NA-induced increase in Agrp and Npy mRNA expression is abolished if NA terminals in the ARH are eliminated by the injection of saporin-conjugated anti-dopamine-β-hydroxylase.
source: This effect is abolished if NA terminals in the ARH are eliminated by the injection of saporin-conjugated anti-dopamine-β-hydroxylase (anti-dβh), a selective NA immunotoxin.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Fraley and Ritter, 2003).

claim: The immunotoxin eliminated a large number of neurons in the ventrolateral medulla (A1/C1 cell groups), which have been identified as mediators of glucoprivic feeding.
source: Specifically, the immunotoxin also eliminated a large number of neurons in the ventrolateral medulla (A1/C1 cell groups), which have been identified as mediators of glucoprivic feeding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Fraley and Ritter, 2003).

claim: The LC plays a key role in mobilizing the required energy to face anticipated physical challenges, such as to obtain rewards.
source: Based on in vivo electrophysiological recordings in primates, it is hypothesized that the LC plays a key role in mobilizing the required energy to face anticipated physical challenges, such as to obtain rewards (Bouret and Richmond, 2015; Varazzani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the LC model, the LC activity is directly related to the energetic need that is required to master the challenge.
source: In this model, the LC activity is directly related to the energetic need that is required to master the challenge.
evidence: This is part of a hypothesis based on cited research.

claim: NA release in the ARH might promote compensatory energy intake.
source: NA release in the ARH might then promote compensatory energy intake.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the LC model.

claim: NA and adrenalin activate three major classes of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): α1-, α2- and β-ARs.
source: On the cellular level NA action can be mediated by a variety of ARs that can inhibit or excite neurons. NA and adrenalin activate three major classes of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): α1-, α2- and β-ARs (Hein, 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Excitatory α1-ARs are coupled to Gq/11 and mediate an increase in intracellular Ca2+ levels and closure of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs).
source: While excitatory α1-ARs are coupled to Gq/11 and mediate an increase in intracellular Ca2+ levels and closure of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs), inhibitory α2-ARs couple to Gi/o leading to inhibition of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs) and opening of GIRKs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AR signaling.

claim: Inhibitory α2-ARs couple to Gi/o leading to inhibition of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs) and opening of GIRKs.
source: While excitatory α1-ARs are coupled to Gq/11 and mediate an increase in intracellular Ca2+ levels and closure of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs), inhibitory α2-ARs couple to Gi/o leading to inhibition of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs) and opening of GIRKs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AR signaling.

claim: β-ARs mediate excitation via activation of Gs proteins and subsequent elevation of internal Ca2+ concentrations and opening of VGCCs.
source: β-ARs mediate excitation via activation of Gs proteins and subsequent elevation of internal Ca2+ concentrations and opening of VGCCs (Marzo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Most NPY/AgRP neurons were spontaneously active under control conditions.
source: As described previously, most NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were spontaneously active under control conditions (NPY/AgRP neurons: (Baver et al., 2014; Steculorum et al., 2015; Tsaousidou et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2015); POMC neurons: (Ernst et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2015; Newton et al., 2013; Plum et al., 2006; Zhang and van den Pol, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most POMC neurons were spontaneously active under control conditions.
source: As described previously, most NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were spontaneously active under control conditions (NPY/AgRP neurons: (Baver et al., 2014; Steculorum et al., 2015; Tsaousidou et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2015); POMC neurons: (Ernst et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2015; Newton et al., 2013; Plum et al., 2006; Zhang and van den Pol, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bath-applied 10 µM NA depolarized orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Bath-applied 10 µM NA had clear opposite effects on these functionally antagonistic neuron types. NA depolarized orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons and increased their action potential frequency from 2.0 ± 0.9 Hz to 5.0 ± 1.0 Hz (Figure 1A,B; NPY/AgRP neurons, Wilcoxon matched pairs signed rank test, n = 8, p=0.0012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bath-applied 10 µM NA increased NPY/AgRP neuron action potential frequency from 2.0 ± 0.9 Hz to 5.0 ± 1.0 Hz.
source: NA depolarized orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons and increased their action potential frequency from 2.0 ± 0.9 Hz to 5.0 ± 1.0 Hz (Figure 1A,B; NPY/AgRP neurons, Wilcoxon matched pairs signed rank test, n = 8, p=0.0012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bath-applied 10 µM NA hyperpolarized anorexigenic POMC neurons.
source: In contrast, NA clearly hyperpolarized anorexigenic POMC neurons and drastically reduced or even abolished spontaneous generation of action potentials from 3.5 ± 1.1 to 0.7 ± 0.7 Hz (Figure 1A,B; POMC neurons, Wilcoxon matched pairs signed rank test, n = 8, p=0.0156).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bath-applied 10 µM NA reduced POMC neuron action potential frequency from 3.5 ± 1.1 to 0.7 ± 0.7 Hz.
source: In contrast, NA clearly hyperpolarized anorexigenic POMC neurons and drastically reduced or even abolished spontaneous generation of action potentials from 3.5 ± 1.1 to 0.7 ± 0.7 Hz (Figure 1A,B; POMC neurons, Wilcoxon matched pairs signed rank test, n = 8, p=0.0156).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In both NPY/AgRP and POMC neuron types, the NA effect had a rapid onset and was readily reversible.
source: In both neuron types, the NA effect had a rapid onset and was readily reversible.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: NA depolarized the membrane potential of NPY/AgRP neurons starting at a concentration of 100 nM.
source: NA depolarized the membrane potential and increased the action potential frequency starting at a concentration of 100 nM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-response data shown in Figure 2.

claim: NA increased the action potential frequency of NPY/AgRP neurons starting at a concentration of 100 nM.
source: NA depolarized the membrane potential and increased the action potential frequency starting at a concentration of 100 nM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-response data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At 10 µM NA, the average firing frequency of NPY/AgRP neurons increased from 2.2 ± 0.8 Hz to 4.7 ± 0.8 Hz.
source: The maximal responses were observed at 10 µM where NA increased the average firing frequency from 2.2 ± 0.8 Hz to 4.7 ± 0.8 Hz (Figure 2B; paired t-test, n = 8, p<0.0001) and depolarized the membrane by 5.1 ± 1.0 mV (Figure 2C; paired t-test, n = 8, p=0.0011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At 10 µM NA, the membrane of NPY/AgRP neurons was depolarized by 5.1 ± 1.0 mV.
source: The maximal responses were observed at 10 µM where NA increased the average firing frequency from 2.2 ± 0.8 Hz to 4.7 ± 0.8 Hz (Figure 2B; paired t-test, n = 8, p<0.0001) and depolarized the membrane by 5.1 ± 1.0 mV (Figure 2C; paired t-test, n = 8, p=0.0011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The concentration-response relation for membrane depolarization in NPY/AgRP neurons had an EC50 of 1.9 µM (1.1–3.2 µM; n = 8).
source: The concentration-response relations had EC50s of 1.9 µM (1.1–3.2 µM; n = 8) and 1.5 µM (0.8–2.8 µM; n = 8), respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting concentration-response data.

claim: The concentration-response relation for increase in firing frequency in NPY/AgRP neurons had an EC50 of 1.5 µM (0.8–2.8 µM; n = 8).
source: The concentration-response relations had EC50s of 1.9 µM (1.1–3.2 µM; n = 8) and 1.5 µM (0.8–2.8 µM; n = 8), respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting concentration-response data.

claim: Synaptically isolated NPY/AgRP neurons responded similarly to the application of NA as without synaptic blockers.
source: Synaptically isolated NPY/AgRP neurons responded similarly to the application of NA as without synaptic blockers (Figure 2D,E), demonstrating that the excitatory NA effect is mediated by cell-intrinsic ARs and the applied GABA and glutamate antagonists do not directly interfere with the AR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The excitatory NA effect on NPY/AgRP neurons is mediated by cell-intrinsic ARs.
source: Synaptically isolated NPY/AgRP neurons responded similarly to the application of NA as without synaptic blockers (Figure 2D,E), demonstrating that the excitatory NA effect is mediated by cell-intrinsic ARs and the applied GABA and glutamate antagonists do not directly interfere with the AR.
evidence: This is an inference from the synaptic isolation experiments.

claim: The NA inhibition of POMC neurons started at 100 nM.
source: The NA inhibition started at 100 nM and the maximal inhibitory effect was reached at 10 µM where NA hyperpolarized the membrane potential by 18.6 ± 3.2 mV (Figure 3B; paired t-test, n = 8; p=0.0007) and increased the conductance from 647 ± 106 pS to 1546 ± 266 pS (Figure 3C; paired t-test, n = 8; p=0.0029).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-response data shown in Figure 3.

claim: At 10 µM NA, the membrane potential of POMC neurons was hyperpolarized by 18.6 ± 3.2 mV.
source: The NA inhibition started at 100 nM and the maximal inhibitory effect was reached at 10 µM where NA hyperpolarized the membrane potential by 18.6 ± 3.2 mV (Figure 3B; paired t-test, n = 8; p=0.0007) and increased the conductance from 647 ± 106 pS to 1546 ± 266 pS (Figure 3C; paired t-test, n = 8; p=0.0029).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: At 10 µM NA, the conductance of POMC neurons increased from 647 ± 106 pS to 1546 ± 266 pS.
source: The NA inhibition started at 100 nM and the maximal inhibitory effect was reached at 10 µM where NA hyperpolarized the membrane potential by 18.6 ± 3.2 mV (Figure 3B; paired t-test, n = 8; p=0.0007) and increased the conductance from 647 ± 106 pS to 1546 ± 266 pS (Figure 3C; paired t-test, n = 8; p=0.0029).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The NA effect on POMC neurons developed rapidly and was reversible.
source: The NA effect developed rapidly and was reversible.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: After application of high concentration NA, the wash out induced a slow, sustained (~10 min) rebound excitation in POMC neurons.
source: However, after application of high concentration, the wash out of NA induced a slow, sustained (~10 min) rebound excitation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: NA concentrations higher than 10 µM did not further increase the effect on POMC neurons.
source: NA concentrations higher than 10 µM did not further increase the effect.
evidence: This is an observation from concentration-response experiments.

claim: The concentration-response relation for membrane hyperpolarization in POMC neurons had an EC50 of 0.9 µM (0.6–1.5 µM; n = 8).
source: The normalized concentration-response relations for conductance increase and membrane hyperpolarization were well fit with a sigmoidal relation (Equation 1), with EC50s of 0.9 µM (0.6–1.5 µM; n = 8) and 1.3 µM (1.0–1.9 µM; n = 8) for the hyperpolarization and the conductance density, respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting concentration-response data.

claim: The concentration-response relation for conductance density increase in POMC neurons had an EC50 of 1.3 µM (1.0–1.9 µM; n = 8).
source: The normalized concentration-response relations for conductance increase and membrane hyperpolarization were well fit with a sigmoidal relation (Equation 1), with EC50s of 0.9 µM (0.6–1.5 µM; n = 8) and 1.3 µM (1.0–1.9 µM; n = 8) for the hyperpolarization and the conductance density, respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting concentration-response data.

claim: In experiments in which the GABAergic and glutamatergic input of the POMC neurons was pharmacologically blocked, the NA response was slightly decreased (~16%) compared to recordings without synaptic blockers present.
source: In experiments in which the GABAergic and glutamatergic input of the POMC neurons was pharmacologically blocked, the NA response was slightly decreased (~16%) compared to recordings without synaptic blockers present, suggesting a small presynaptic contribution by NA responsive neurons, which project on POMC neurons (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: There is a small presynaptic contribution by NA responsive neurons, which project on POMC neurons.
source: In experiments in which the GABAergic and glutamatergic input of the POMC neurons was pharmacologically blocked, the NA response was slightly decreased (~16%) compared to recordings without synaptic blockers present, suggesting a small presynaptic contribution by NA responsive neurons, which project on POMC neurons (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is an inference from the synaptic isolation experiments.

claim: The presynaptic contribution to POMC neuron inhibition is likely caused by the mono-directional inhibitory synaptic innervation of POMC neurons by NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Given the excitatory effect of NA on NPY/AgRP neurons, this effect is likely caused by their mono-directional inhibitory synaptic innervation of POMC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on known circuit connectivity and the excitatory effect of NA on NPY/AgRP neurons.

claim: Comparing POMC versus NPY transcriptional profiles yielded 4482 significantly differentially expressed genes (FC≥2, p≤0.01).
source: Comparing POMC versus NPY transcriptional profiles yielded 4482 significantly differentially expressed genes (FC≥2, p≤0.01).
evidence: This is from the transcriptomic analysis performed in the study.

claim: Pomc was enriched 147-fold in the POMC-expressing population.
source: Within this pool, Pomc was enriched 147-fold in the corresponding population, with Npy and Agrp being higher expressed in NPY-derived samples, but not in a statistically significant way (Figure 4A, supplemental file 1).
evidence: This is from the transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Npy and Agrp were higher expressed in NPY-derived samples, but not in a statistically significant way.
source: Within this pool, Pomc was enriched 147-fold in the corresponding population, with Npy and Agrp being higher expressed in NPY-derived samples, but not in a statistically significant way (Figure 4A, supplemental file 1).
evidence: This is from the transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NPY/AgRP neurons expressed all subtypes of ARs, except α1D- and α2B- ARs.
source: NPY/AgRP neurons expressed all subtypes of ARs, except α1D- and α2B- ARs.
evidence: This is from the transcriptomic analysis.

claim: POMC neurons only expressed α1A- and α2A- ARs, albeit to a lower magnitude.
source: POMC neurons only expressed α1A- and α2A- ARs, albeit to a lower magnitude (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from the transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were positive for Adra1a expression.
source: Both NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were positive for Adra1a and Adra2a expression, with Adra1a being expressed in more NPY/AgRP neurons, compared to POMC neurons (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is from RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Both NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were positive for Adra2a expression.
source: Both NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were positive for Adra1a and Adra2a expression, with Adra1a being expressed in more NPY/AgRP neurons, compared to POMC neurons (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is from RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Adra1a was expressed in more NPY/AgRP neurons, compared to POMC neurons.
source: Both NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons were positive for Adra1a and Adra2a expression, with Adra1a being expressed in more NPY/AgRP neurons, compared to POMC neurons (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is from RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Adra2a was expressed to a similar extent between NPY/AgRP and POMC populations.
source: Adra2a was however expressed to a similar extent between the two populations (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is from RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Adrb1 was expressed only in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Adrb1 and Adrb2 were expressed only in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is from RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adrb2 was expressed only in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Adrb1 and Adrb2 were expressed only in NPY/AgRP neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is from RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARs are differentially expressed between NPY and POMC neurons within the hypothalamus.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that ARs are differentially expressed between NPY and POMC neurons within the hypothalamus, possibly mediating any distinct modulatory effects of NA on these populations.
evidence: This is an inference from the transcriptomic and in situ hybridization data.

claim: During the combined application of prazosine and yohimbine the excitatory NA effect was completely blocked in 44% (4 of 9) of the NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: During the combined application of prazosine and yohimbine the excitatory NA effect was completely blocked in 44% (4 of 9; Figure 5A) and significantly (~60%) attenuated in 55% (5 of 9; Figure 5B) of the NPY/AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: During the combined application of prazosine and yohimbine the excitatory NA effect was significantly (~60%) attenuated in 55% (5 of 9) of the NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: During the combined application of prazosine and yohimbine the excitatory NA effect was completely blocked in 44% (4 of 9; Figure 5A) and significantly (~60%) attenuated in 55% (5 of 9; Figure 5B) of the NPY/AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The excitatory NA effect in NPY/AgRP neurons can be mediated solely by α1-ARs or by the co-activation of α1-ARs and β-ARs.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that the excitatory NA effect in NPY/AgRP neurons can be mediated solely by α1-ARs or by the co-activation of α1-ARs and β-ARs.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments with prazosine and yohimbine.

claim: The selective α1A-AR agonist A-61603 (1 µM) depolarized the membrane potential and increased the AP frequency in NPY/AgRP neurons similarly as a subsequent NA application.
source: The selective α1A-AR agonist A-61603 (1 µM) depolarized the membrane potential and increased the AP frequency in NPY/AgRP neurons similarly as a subsequent NA application (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The selective α1A-AR antagonist WB4101 (100 nM) abolished the excitatory NA response in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: In line with these data, we found that the selective α1A-AR antagonist WB4101 (100 nM) abolished the excitatory NA response (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Application of WB4101 resulted in an inhibitory effect, suggesting baseline activation of α1A-AR in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Application of WB4101 resulted in an inhibitory effect, suggesting baseline activation of α1A-AR.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments with WB4101.

claim: The subtype-specific α1B,D-AR antagonist chloro-ethyl-clonidine (CEC; 100 nM) did not block or alter the NA action on NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: The subtype-specific α1B,D-AR antagonist chloro-ethyl-clonidine (CEC; 100 nM) did not block or alter the NA action (Figure 6E,F), suggesting that α1B,D-ARs do not contribute to the excitation.
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: α1B,D-ARs do not contribute to the excitation of NPY/AgRP neurons by NA.
source: The subtype-specific α1B,D-AR antagonist chloro-ethyl-clonidine (CEC; 100 nM) did not block or alter the NA action (Figure 6E,F), suggesting that α1B,D-ARs do not contribute to the excitation.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments with CEC.

claim: NA excites NPY/AgRP neurons via activation of α1A-ARs.
source: Taken together, these data show that NA excites NPY/AgRP neurons via activation of α1A-ARs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: In the presence of WB4101, NA had an inhibitory effect on the NPY/AgRP membrane potential.
source: In the presence of WB4101 NA had an inhibitory effect on the membrane potential, which was eliminated by the α2A-AR antagonist BRL44408 (10 µM).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The inhibitory effect of NA on NPY/AgRP neurons in the presence of WB4101 was eliminated by the α2A-AR antagonist BRL44408 (10 µM).
source: In the presence of WB4101 NA had an inhibitory effect on the membrane potential, which was eliminated by the α2A-AR antagonist BRL44408 (10 µM).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The inhibitory α2A-ARs are functional in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: These data show that the inhibitory α2A-ARs are functional in NPY/AgRP neurons and also support the notion that excitatory β-ARs are activated by NA, as indicated in the first set of experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments with WB4101 and BRL44408.

claim: Excitatory β-ARs are activated by NA in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: These data show that the inhibitory α2A-ARs are functional in NPY/AgRP neurons and also support the notion that excitatory β-ARs are activated by NA, as indicated in the first set of experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: All receptors identified by cell-type specific transcriptomics are functional in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that all receptors, which were identified by cell-type specific transcriptomics, are functional in NPY/AgRP neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from combining transcriptomic and pharmacological data.

claim: The excitatory NA effect observed in virtually all NPY/AgRP neurons is predominantly mediated by α1A-ARs and might be in some neurons co-mediated by β-ARs.
source: The excitatory NA effect that we observed in virtually all neurons is predominantly mediated by α1A-ARs and might be in some neurons co-mediated by β-ARs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The activation of excitatory AR interferes with the activation of inhibitory α2A-ARs in NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: The activation of excitatory AR interferes with the activation of inhibitory α2A-ARs.
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments showing that blocking excitatory receptors reveals inhibitory effects.

claim: The α2A-AR antagonist BRL 44408 (10 µM) blocked the NA mediated inhibitory effect on POMC neurons.
source: The α2A-AR antagonist BRL 44408 (10 µM) blocked the NA mediated inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Application of 10 µM BRL 44408 alone did not significantly alter the recorded electrophysiological properties of POMC neurons, suggesting no baseline activity of α2A-ARs.
source: Application of 10 µM BRL 44408 alone, did not significantly alter the recorded electrophysiological properties, suggesting no baseline activity of α2A-ARs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The specific α2B-AR antagonist ARC 239 (1 µM) did not change the inhibitory effect of NA on POMC neurons.
source: The specific α2B-AR antagonist ARC 239 (1 µM) did not change the inhibitory effect of NA, which suggests that the inhibitory NA action is solely mediated by α2A-ARs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The inhibitory NA action on POMC neurons is solely mediated by α2A-ARs.
source: The specific α2B-AR antagonist ARC 239 (1 µM) did not change the inhibitory effect of NA, which suggests that the inhibitory NA action is solely mediated by α2A-ARs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments with ARC 239.

claim: When the inhibitory α2-ARs were blocked by yohimbine (5 µM), NA excited POMC neurons.
source: When the inhibitory α2-ARs were blocked by yohimbine (5 µM), NA excited POMC neurons (Figure 7D; paired t-test, n = 10, p=0.0168).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The excitation of POMC neurons by NA in the presence of yohimbine was completely abolished by the α1-AR antagonist prazosine (5 µM).
source: This excitation was completely abolished by the α1-AR antagonist prazosine (5 µM), showing the functionality of α1-ARs in POMC neurons (Figure 7E; paired t-test, n = 6, p=0.2467).
evidence: This is from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: α1-ARs are functional in POMC neurons.
source: This excitation was completely abolished by the α1-AR antagonist prazosine (5 µM), showing the functionality of α1-ARs in POMC neurons (Figure 7E; paired t-test, n = 6, p=0.2467).
evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The NA-induced inhibition of POMC neurons is mediated by α2A-AR and can mask the activation of excitatory α1-ARs.
source: Taken together, our results show that the NA-induced inhibition of POMC neurons is mediated by α2A-AR and can mask the activation of excitatory α1-ARs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: NA directly modulates NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons of the ARH for the first time.
source: Here, we show for the first time that NA directly modulates NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons of the ARH, which are key components of the neuronal circuits that control food intake and energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: The strong differential modulation of NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons by NA was reproducible in virtually all recorded neurons.
source: The strong differential modulation, which was reproducible in virtually all recorded neurons, is remarkable, since other important fuel sensing modulators like insulin, leptin, glucose, oleic acid and UDP typically affect only a subpopulation of these neurons (Jo et al., 2009; Parton et al., 2007; Steculorum et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data compared to previous studies.

claim: Other important fuel sensing modulators like insulin, leptin, glucose, oleic acid and UDP typically affect only a subpopulation of NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons.
source: The strong differential modulation, which was reproducible in virtually all recorded neurons, is remarkable, since other important fuel sensing modulators like insulin, leptin, glucose, oleic acid and UDP typically affect only a subpopulation of these neurons (Jo et al., 2009; Parton et al., 2007; Steculorum et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The clear differential NA modulation of functionally antagonistic neuron types should generate a strong orexigenic drive on the homeostatic circuits of the ARH.
source: On the network and systems level, this clear differential NA modulation of functionally antagonistic neuron types should generate a strong orexigenic drive on the homeostatic circuits of the ARH.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings about opposite effects on orexigenic and anorexigenic neurons.

claim: Injection of NA into the third ventricle increased food intake.
source: This conclusion is consistent with early behavioral experiments from Clark et al. (1988) showing that injection of NA into the third ventricle increased food intake.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous behavioral research.

claim: Blockade of α2-AR attenuated the NA-induced feeding behavior.
source: Furthermore, the authors showed that blockade of α2-AR attenuated the NA-induced feeding behavior, which is in line with our finding that satiety signaling POMC- neurons are inhibited by NA via α2-AR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous behavioral research (Clark et al., 1988).

claim: The modulatory effects of NA were observed in synaptically isolated neurons, suggesting that NA directly activated intrinsically expressed ARs.
source: Since the modulatory effects of NA were observed in synaptically isolated neurons, the data suggest that NA directly activated intrinsically expressed ARs.
evidence: This is an inference from the synaptic isolation experiments.

claim: The cell type-specific transcriptomic data is in line with recent data from Henry et al. (2015).
source: Our cell type-specific transcriptomic data showed expression of excitatory and inhibitory receptor subtypes in both NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons, which is in line with recent data from Henry et al. (2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research.

claim: In NPY/AgRP neurons, the robust excitation is mediated by excitatory α1A- and β-ARs.
source: While in NPY/AgRP the robust excitation is mediated by excitatory α1A- and β-ARs, α2A-ARs mediated the strong inhibition in POMC neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: α2A-ARs mediated the strong inhibition in POMC neurons.
source: While in NPY/AgRP the robust excitation is mediated by excitatory α1A- and β-ARs, α2A-ARs mediated the strong inhibition in POMC neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Simultaneous expression of excitatory and inhibitory adrenergic receptors has been found in neurons of the LC.
source: Simultaneous expression of excitatory and inhibitory adrenergic receptors has been found in neurons of the LC.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the discussion.

claim: In juvenile mice, mRNA for excitatory α1A,B,D- and inhibitory α2A,B,C-ARs has been detected in LC neurons and application of NA caused excitation.
source: In juvenile mice, mRNA for excitatory α1A,B,D- and inhibitory α2A,B,C-ARs has been detected and application of NA caused excitation, while in adult mice NA hyperpolarizes LC neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Osborne et al., 2002).

claim: In adult mice, NA hyperpolarizes LC neurons.
source: In juvenile mice, mRNA for excitatory α1A,B,D- and inhibitory α2A,B,C-ARs has been detected and application of NA caused excitation, while in adult mice NA hyperpolarizes LC neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Osborne et al., 2002).

claim: In adult LC neurons, α1-ARs attenuate the NA-induced hyperpolarization.
source: Here, α1-ARs attenuate the NA-induced hyperpolarization (Osborne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: POMC neurons might change their response to NA during development.
source: As in LC neurons, POMC neurons might change their response to NA during development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the LC neuron example.

claim: In the ARH, developmental changes of electrophysiological responses to leptin have been described for NPY/AgRP neurons.
source: In the ARH developmental changes of electrophysiological responses to leptin have been described for NPY/AgRP neurons (Baquero et al., 2014; Nilsson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Simultaneous expression of excitatory and inhibitory ARs has been found in dentate neurons of the human cerebellum.
source: Simultaneous expression of excitatory and inhibitory ARs has also been found in dentate neurons of the human cerebellum (Schambra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In dentate neurons of the human cerebellum, α2B-ARs are thought to modulate excitatory glutamatergic input.
source: Here, α2B-ARs are thought to modulate excitatory glutamatergic input, while α1A,B-ARs may play a role in timing and computation of inhibitory input.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Schambra et al., 2005).

claim: In dentate neurons of the human cerebellum, α1A,B-ARs may play a role in timing and computation of inhibitory input.
source: Here, α2B-ARs are thought to modulate excitatory glutamatergic input, while α1A,B-ARs may play a role in timing and computation of inhibitory input.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Schambra et al., 2005).

claim: Previous studies in dentate neurons of the cerebellum suggested that α1-ARs are expressed on the cell body while α2-ARs are expressed on the terminals.
source: Previous studies in dentate neurons of the cerebellum suggested that α1-ARs are expressed on the cell body while α2-ARs are expressed on the terminals, in order to locally regulate transmitter release (Milner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is evidence from early work that catecholamines can cross the blood brain barrier in the hypothalamus.
source: While the blood brain barrier in adult animals is considered mostly impermeable for catecholamines, there is evidence from early work that catecholamines can cross the blood brain barrier in the hypothalamus (Weil-Malherbe et al., 1959).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The site specific effects of local lesions and local NA injections into the hypothalamus might argue for local, site specific NA release from neurons.
source: However, the site specific effects of local lesions and local NA injections into the hypothalamus might argue for local, site specific NA release from neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from previous lesion and injection studies.

claim: Specific deletion of projections from the ventro-lateral medulla (A1/C1 cell group) is sufficient to eliminate an increase in AgRP and NPY mRNA expression in response to glucoprivation induced by 2-DG.
source: Specific deletion of projections from the ventro-lateral medulla (A1/C1 cell group) is sufficient to eliminate an increase in AgRP and NPY mRNA expression in response to glucoprivation induced by 2-DG.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research (Fraley and Ritter, 2003).

claim: Homeostatic feeding in response to local hypoglycemia in the hindbrain was decreased by specific deletion of projections from the ventro-lateral medulla.
source: Furthermore, homeostatic feeding in response to local hypoglycemia in the hindbrain was decreased (Fraley and Ritter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NA release into the ARH upon LC activation generates an orexigenic drive to compensate for the required energy.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, our data suggest that NA release into the ARH upon LC activation generates an orexigenic drive to compensate for the required energy.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data in the context of the LC model.

claim: NA injections into the hypothalamus elicit food intake.
source: In line with this hypothesis, previous studies revealed that NA injections into the hypothalamus elicit food intake (Booth, 1967; Leibowitz, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral research.

claim: Insulin selectively decreased α2-AR expression in the ARH and dorsomedial hypothalamus.
source: While insulin selectively decreased α2-AR expression in the ARH and dorsomedial hypothalamus (Levin et al., 1998), leptin inhibits NA release in rats (Brunetti et al., 1999; Francis et al., 2004), Both effects would augment the net anorexigenic signal.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Leptin inhibits NA release in rats.
source: While insulin selectively decreased α2-AR expression in the ARH and dorsomedial hypothalamus (Levin et al., 1998), leptin inhibits NA release in rats (Brunetti et al., 1999; Francis et al., 2004), Both effects would augment the net anorexigenic signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both insulin decreasing α2-AR expression and leptin inhibiting NA release would augment the net anorexigenic signal.
source: While insulin selectively decreased α2-AR expression in the ARH and dorsomedial hypothalamus (Levin et al., 1998), leptin inhibits NA release in rats (Brunetti et al., 1999; Francis et al., 2004), Both effects would augment the net anorexigenic signal.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited effects of insulin and leptin.

claim: Obese mice that lack the gene to produce leptin (Lepob/ob) exhibit increased NA levels within the hypothalamus.
source: In support of the latter relation, obese mice that lack the gene to produce leptin (Lepob/ob) exhibit increased NA levels within the hypothalamus, which further decreases the anorexigenic signal (Oltmans, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased NA levels in Lepob/ob mice further decreases the anorexigenic signal.
source: In support of the latter relation, obese mice that lack the gene to produce leptin (Lepob/ob) exhibit increased NA levels within the hypothalamus, which further decreases the anorexigenic signal (Oltmans, 1983).
evidence: This is an inference from the cited research on Lepob/ob mice.

claim: Several drugs that were developed to modify food intake act on the monoaminergic transmitter system in the brain.
source: Several drugs that were developed to modify food intake, act on the monoaminergic transmitter system in the brain.
evidence: This is general knowledge about anti-obesity drugs.

claim: Anti-obesity drugs often cause strong side effects because the molecular and cellular targets that mediate their effects are often not clearly identified.
source: Since the molecular and cellular targets that mediate the effects of these drugs are often not clearly identified, they often cause strong side effects (Hainer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The current findings reveal cell type-specific pathways that mediate NA modulation in the ARH and might help to better define specific targets for anti-obesity drugs.
source: Since the current findings reveal cell type-specific pathways that mediate NA modulation in the ARH they might help to better define specific targets for anti-obesity drugs.
